title: Vegetation succession redirects microbial carbon metabolism via conserved core CAZyme gene families to enhance soil carbon molecular complexity
content:

Abstract

Understanding how core carbohydrate-active enzyme (CAZyme) gene families regulate soil organic carbon (SOC) molecular diversity and persistence remains a central challenge in linking vegetation succession to long-term carbon storage. We investigated this dynamic across a 130-year glacial retreat chronosequence, spanning six plant community stages from grass–shrub communities to primary forests, using metagenomics and SOC molecular profiling to resolve vegetation-driven microbial controls on carbon complexity. As plant communities transitioned from shrubs to forests, microbial resource allocation changed significantly. The 37 identified persistent core CAZyme families coordinated this metabolic reorganization through both direct and indirect regulatory pathways (R 2 = 0.758). In these pathways, core families directly modulated enzymatic transformation kinetics by optimizing enzyme–substrate affinity, while indirectly shaping SOC dynamics by dictating the functional potential of the broader microbial CAZyme repertoire. Microbial communities systematically reduced investment in extracellular plant polysaccharide decomposition (e.g., declines in CBM66 by 30.1% and PL22 by 19.2%). Instead, these communities increasingly directed metabolic effort towards the intracellular processing of necromass, a process evidenced by the significant (p < 0.05) rebounds in GH177 and CE4 abundance during the late-successional Prim.6 stage. This functional reorientation directly governed the assembly of SOC molecular architecture by shifting the network from modular clusters (modularity: 0.93; density: 0.023) to highly integrated webs with an average degree of 12.81. Furthermore, the 10-fold increase in available phosphorus acted as a stoichiometric switch that modulated the abundance of these core gene families and fundamentally drove the trajectory of microbially mediated SOC stabilization. Our study reveals that during vegetation succession, core CAZyme families act as central metabolic hubs. By redirecting microbial carbon metabolism towards enhanced intracellular recycling pathways, amplified by soil phosphorus availability, this mechanism enhances molecular network complexity and extends the microbial carbon pump concept. Crucially, in the context of global environmental change, shifts in atmospheric nutrient deposition may alter exogenous nutrient supply, with potential consequences for the carbon sequestration capacity of high-alpine soils. These results highlight that the metabolic sensitivity of microbially driven carbon sinks must be explicitly accounted for in future ecological conservation strategies for fragile alpine environments.
